progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From Year 11: neurons carry nerve impulses; hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood; the brain coordinates responses; enzymes have an active site and an optimum temperature and pH. Not assumed: homeostasis, set point, tolerance range, the five components, thermoreceptor, hypothalamus, effector, negative and positive feedback.
progression.startsWith: Trace stimulus, receptor, control and effector. The video opens: Right now you're probably in a room at about twenty-two degrees, and your body is losing heat to it every second.
progression.stopsAfter: defining homeostasis as keeping the internal environment relatively stable within a tolerance range around a set point, and saying why (enzyme activity); naming and ordering the five components with their jobs for a fall in body temperature (thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus, hypothalamus as control centre, shivering muscles and narrowing skin arterioles as effectors, heat made and kept as the response); explaining why the loop is negative (the response opposes the change) and easing as the variable returns (signals weaken and the extra response fades to what is needed, not to zero; small fluctuations can occur around the set point); contrasting positive feedback (amplifies a change until an end point, blood clotting); mapping the same template onto rising blood glucose (pancreas as receptor and control centre, insulin, liver and muscle cells as effectors); constructing a loop from a written description and interpreting a two-line graph, keeping the regulated internal variable separate from the external change.
progression.nextLesson: how endotherms detect heat and the main ways they lose or keep it (route entry bio-m8-b02).

teaching.task: You lose heat to a 22 °C room every second, yet your core temperature stays close to 37 °C. What detects the drift, what decides, and what corrects it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the range matters (enzymes; 2); how each part leads to the next (4); why the loop is negative (direction; 5) and why it stops itself (weakening signals; 5); why positive feedback cannot hold a variable (it amplifies until an end point; 6). Attention: a question about the learner's own body (1), a familiar machine (3), a contrast (6). Visual medium: one loop ring that fills slot by slot with real structures and is reused for glucose and both attempts. Apply: construct (10a), interpret (10c). Remember: the mnemonic and the minus-sign arrow.
teaching.conversationalApproach: You are probably sitting in a room at about 22 degrees, losing heat every second, yet your core temperature stays close to 37, so the question is how negative feedback keeps conditions in range: what detects the drift, what decides and what fixes it. Homeostasis is keeping the internal environment relatively stable, with core temperature wobbling within a narrow band, the tolerance range, around a set point. A heater with a thermostat shows the same loop with its set point, sensor and switch. The body's loop has five parts, built in a cold wind: the stimulus (body temperature starting to fall), thermoreceptors in the skin and hypothalamus as receptors, the hypothalamus as control centre, the skin arterioles and muscles as effectors, and the response that makes more heat and loses less. It is negative because the response opposes the change, and as temperature returns the receptors detect less change and the response eases. Positive feedback is the contrast: platelets at a torn vessel call in more platelets until the hole is plugged. The same template fits blood glucose, where the pancreas is both receptor and control centre and insulin brings glucose back down. Two exam checks follow (which variable inside the body, which way the response pushes), then the memory aid Some Really Cool Elephants Run and two exam questions with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Right now you're probably in a room at about twenty-two degrees, and your body is losing heat to it every second. Yet your core temperature stays close to thirty-seven. Something keeps detecting that drift and correcting it. So what detects it, what decides, and what does the fixing?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a construct item from a written description (the dotpoint's first verb). 10c is an interpret item from a two-line graph (the second verb, and the 2019 Q29 trap). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 s each): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the card as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ1-01 (p 56): "construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)" with the listed examples "temperature (ACSBL098)" and "glucose". Temperature carries the build (scenes 4 and 5, attempt 2); glucose is the transfer (scene 7). "Construct" is attempt 1; "interpret" is attempt 2. "Range of sources": a thermostat model (3), a loop diagram (4), a trace graph (5, attempt 2) and a written description (attempt 1).

design.visualSystem: One loop ring owns the frame from scene 4: five slots on a circle (stimulus at the top, then clockwise receptor, control centre, effector, response), joined by curved arrows, with a return arrow from response back to stimulus marked with a minus sign in scene 5. Each slot holds one small painted plate or a short label, never a text box standing in for a structure. The ring persists, dimmed, through scenes 6 to 8 and reappears small in 11. A trace panel (the coded `lineGraph`: variable against time, a shaded tolerance band and a dashed set point line) sits to the right in scenes 2, 5 and attempt 2. People are never drawn: there is no body outline; the internal variable is shown by the skin cross-section plate, the brain plate and the thermometer plate. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey when a new one writes.
